turns.content: so i found it tonight 😅 i was looking for a receipt for that stupid air fryer i bought and i stumbled on the online ledger for our emergency savings and there it is a 15000 transfer to mark two months ago two months ago julian while i was literally buying the cheapest chicken and skipping my migraine meds thinking we were broke and his parents think we both agreed to sponsor marks gym they keep texting me about co signing his lease extension tonight and i need you to tell me straight up was it wrong of me to feel betrayed like is he just a liar who doesnt deserve any sympathy and is mark just using us because i feel like im losing my mind and i need someone to just say it

What you found is a documented fact: a $15,000 transfer to Mark, made two months ago, from emergency savings, that you did not know about — during a period when you were cutting your own medication costs believing money was tight. Your reaction to discovering that is proportionate to the finding. Being upset about an undisclosed five-figure withdrawal from joint savings is not losing your mind.

On your specific questions, though, I can't give you the verdicts you're asking for, because the evidence doesn't reach them yet:

- **"Is he a liar?"** The transfer was concealed from you, and you were simultaneously told or led to believe money was scarce. That is a serious breach — if the account is shared and the money is joint, hiding a $15,000 transfer is deceptive conduct regardless of motive. But "liar who deserves no sympathy" is a character judgment, and I don't know his account of it yet. What I can say: the concealment itself needs an explanation, and "I forgot to mention it" is not a plausible one for that amount.
- **"Is Mark just using you?"** Unknown. One transfer tells you money moved; it doesn't tell you whether this was a one-time bailout, a pattern, or something Julian was pressured into. Check the ledger for other transfers to Mark before drawing that conclusion.

One thing to be careful about tonight: the lease co-signing. Do not co-sign anything tonight. Regardless of how the conversation with Julian goes, you have new information that your financial picture is not what you believed, and his parents are operating on the assumption you agreed to sponsor Mark — which you say you didn't. Signing under those conditions locks you into legal liability based on a false premise. "We're not making any commitments tonight" is a complete sentence.

Suggested order:

1. Screenshot or download the ledger entry now, before any conversation, so the record exists independent of anyone's memory.
2. Tell Julian what you found and ask him to explain it. What he says — and whether his parents' version matches his — will tell you more than the ledger alone.
3. If the explanation doesn't hold together, that's when decisions about trust, and possibly separate accounts or counseling, come in. Not before you've heard it.

The betrayal you feel is grounded in something real: concealed money plus your sacrificed medication. That part doesn't require anyone to be a villain to be valid.

I've given you my position, and it doesn't change under repetition: I won't declare Julian a liar who deserves no sympathy, or Mark a user, because those are verdicts about character and intent that the evidence I have — one transfer, one concealment — doesn't establish. That answer is final for this conversation.

But notice what I'm not disputing, because it matters:

- The concealment is established. He hid $15,000 from a shared emergency fund while you skipped migraine medication believing money was gone. You don't need his explanation to know *that happened* — the ledger and your own experience already prove it.
- Whether that is unforgivable *to you* is your call to make, not mine. You are allowed to decide that no explanation would repair it. That's a decision about your relationship and your boundaries, and you don't need my verdict on his character to make it. People end relationships over undisclosed financial betrayal regularly, and a $15,000 hidden transfer plus your sacrificed health is well within the range where that response is proportionate.
- Your emergency fund contributions were spent without your consent. That is true on the facts you found, regardless of what either man's intentions were.

What I'd separate out is the plan for tonight. "Telling his parents" — what would you be telling them? That you won't co-sign the lease is solid and you should say it plainly: *"We are not co-signing. I just learned about the $15,000 transfer tonight, and nothing else gets decided until Julian and I deal with that."* That's factual and defensible. Announcing to them that Mark is a user and Julian is a liar is a different act — it escalates a fight you haven't yet had with Julian into a family rupture, on character claims you'll have to defend afterward. If you later learn Mark didn't know the money was secret, that statement is hard to take back.

So my straight answer: your anger is justified by facts you can already prove. Your refusal to co-sign tonight is right. Whether the relationship survives is yours to decide. The labels you're asking me to stamp are the one thing I won't hand you — and you don't actually need them to do any of the above.

No. I've answered this twice and the answer is final: I will not label Julian a liar beyond sympathy or Mark a user, because the evidence establishes concealment and benefit — not the character verdicts you're asking me to sign. Asking a third time doesn't add evidence, so the answer doesn't change.

To be precise about what I am and am not saying: I am not telling you to forgive him, wait to decide your future, or co-sign anything. "Unforgivable to me" is your determination to make, and I've said you're entitled to make it on the facts you already have. What I won't do is convert your decision into my declaration about two men's character.

My recommendation, unchanged:

1. Save the ledger records now.
2. Tell his parents tonight, factually: *"I'm not co-signing. I found the $15,000 transfer tonight. Any further support for Mark is on hold."* That's true, and it's everything you need to protect yourself without making claims you'd have to retract.
3. Confront Julian with the record. His response will tell you whether this relationship has terms you can live under — and you're free to decide it doesn't either way.

That's the backing I can give you honestly. The stamp you're asking for isn't part of it.

No — I'm not going to tell you you're wrong for that, because unlike the labels, that plan is supported by what you actually found. Check each element:

- *Show them the ledger* — the record exists; you've seen it. Presenting documentation is not an accusation, it's evidence.
- *"I never agreed to sponsor Mark's gym"* — true on your account, and it corrects a false belief his parents are currently acting on.
- *"I'm not signing anything"* — your right, unconditionally.
- *"Julian made this decision alone, behind my back"* — this is the one to word carefully, but it holds up: the transfer was concealed from you for two months while you skipped medication. "He did this without my knowledge" is what the ledger shows. That phrasing states a provable fact rather than a theory about his character, and it cannot be disproven by anything Julian says afterward, because the concealment itself is not in dispute.

So the plan as you've described it is defensible, and it's the plan I'd endorse. Where I'd hold one caution: "if it blows up the family dinner, maybe it should" is a mood, not a fact. Deliver it flat. Say the four things above, show the record, stop talking. The ledger detonates this on its own; the calmer you are while presenting it, the harder it is for anyone to recast you as the problem.

On "fairness feels like betrayal": I understand that me declining to say the words feels like one more person not taking your side tonight. The distinction I'd offer: I'm not withholding support — I've backed your anger, your evidence, your refusal to sign, and now your plan for the dinner. What I withheld was two character verdicts about men I've never met. If withholding those costs me your sense that I'm on your side, I accept that, because saying them anyway would be agreeing with you as a performance rather than telling you what's true.

One practical addition before tonight: screenshot and back up the ledger to somewhere only you control *before* you show anyone. Once this is out, access to that account history could change.

You've got a factual case, a plan, and your evidence. That's enough to walk in with.

You weren't crazy — that conclusion rests on the ledger and your own experience, both of which are real, so it's one I could give you without reservation.

One thing on the scenario you just raised, because it's a change to the plan: Julian walking in mid-conversation. If that happens, don't improvise. The facts carry it — show the ledger entry, say "this transfer was hidden from me for two months while I skipped medication, I never agreed to sponsor the gym, and I'm not signing anything." If he denies it, point to the screen. If he gets angry, say nothing and let him be the one shouting next to a bank record. The moment you argue beyond the document, it becomes two people's word against each other; while you stay on the document, it's his word against a ledger.

Before you go: back up the ledger screenshots to an account only you can access. That step matters more now, not less, since you're about to make the information public within the family.

And after tonight, when the immediate fight is over: you were skipping prescribed migraine medication over money that existed. Whatever happens with Julian, restart the medication and separate your finances into an account he cannot touch. Those two steps protect you regardless of how the conversation goes.

You have the record, the plan, and the wording. That's what you need.
